You close your fingers around it without answering yet.
You keep your hand open and ask why the insignia has come to you today.
You refuse to let an object turn hesitation into commitment.
Your father's old insignia ends up in your palm. With it comes one sentence: “You're old enough to decide what it means.”
event.family_marine_13_insignia_in_palm_: Ask what he did with it
You ask whether the insignia helped him choose or merely obey.
Look at what it cost the household
You bring the object back to the household, absences, and choices you lived.
Decide it will mean something else
You refuse to inherit the object's meaning along with the object.
You learn what the insignia meant to your father: less a reward than proof that people now expected something from him.
Say you want to join the Marine
You keep the insignia as an inheritance you choose to continue in your own way.
Keep the insignia, not the career
You keep the family story without making it your first profession.
You refuse to let uncertainty at thirteen become a career promise.
The insignia is yours now even if you never wear it. The final decision concerns your future, not the object.
event.family_marine_13_your_future_is_yo: Finally exhale
You realize nobody is turning tonight into automatic enlistment.
Ask why it took so long
You refuse to pretend the years of expectation never weighed on you.
Ask whether the Marine is still possible
You want to know whether freedom includes the right to choose the inheritance.
Your Future Is Yours
The adult beside you puts away the Marine forms and sets an old field compass in front of you: “The direction isn't ours to choose anymore.”
Ask what remains of the ideal
You look for what is still worth keeping in the idea of protection.
Ask what to avoid
You turn family history into warnings as much as inheritance.
Say you want to decide alone
You finally take the decision out of the adults' hands.
Nobody Answers for You
You receive advice, not a verdict. For the first time, no adult turns your family origin into a complete answer.
Choose the Marine anyway
You reject automatic inheritance, then still choose to begin Active in uniform.
Begin Active as a civilian
You enter active life without turning your origin into a profession.
Promise nothing yet
You keep the Marine as a future possibility, but not as your starting point.
Choose the Direction
The compass stays in your pocket whatever you decide. It does not tell you which career to take; only that the direction must be yours.
event.family_marine_13_chest_he_left.cho: You ask for a few minutes before anyone reads over your shoulder.
You refuse to let the inheritance become a solitary conversation.
Ask someone else to read first
You prefer hearing the first sentence in another voice.
event.family_marine_13_chest_he_left.tex: A chest from your father is finally opened before you. Among his service belongings, a journal and a letter bear your name, written long before anyone knew which career you would choose.
event.family_marine_13_chest_he_left_i01: You start with everything he probably would never have put on a plaque.
You follow people rather than ranks through his story.
You look for what he believed at the end rather than what he believed at the beginning.
The journal does not read like a legend: schedules, mistakes, comrades' names, sanctions, successes, and regrets share the same pages.
event.family_marine_13_chest_he_left_i02: Read it as an invitation to continue
You hear a reason to try wearing the uniform differently.
You refuse to turn a family letter into a posthumous order.
You mainly keep what he wanted to stop you from repeating.
The letter does not ask you to become a Marine. It only asks you never to pretend a uniform makes choices simpler than they are.
event.family_marine_13_chest_he_left_i03: You choose the Marine without erasing the pages showing how it can go wrong.
Keep his memory without following his career
You keep his whole story, but your first profession will be your own.
Refuse to let a letter decide
You take the journal as inheritance and refuse to let it become an instruction.
You close the chest but keep the journal. The last thing to decide is whether his service becomes your starting point or only part of your story.
event.family_marine_13_wear_it_better.ch: You refuse a vague confession when it becomes inheritance.
You refuse to let his mistakes become his whole career.
You look for the reason that survived his own criticism.
event.family_marine_13_wear_it_better.ti: Wear It Better Than I Did
event.family_marine_13_wear_it_better.te: Your father takes out his insignia after years of defending, enduring, and sometimes challenging his service. “If you ever wear it, do better than I did where I failed.”
event.family_marine_13_wear_it_better_i0: Keep both
You refuse to choose between condemning the man and idealizing the Marine.
Keep the ideal
You separate what he believed he should do from what he actually managed to do.
Keep the family cost
You refuse to let his public protection erase what it cost the household.
What He Admits
He names absences, one decision made alone, and at least one order he should have challenged earlier. Then he also speaks of people he knows he truly protected.
Take both
You accept his help opening a door without yet deciding how you will walk through it.
Take only the insignia
You accept the family inheritance without taking the professional shortcut.
Give both back
You refuse to let repairing his own story happen through your future.
A Recommendation, Not an Order
He prepared a recommendation allowing you to enter as a Marine recruit when Active begins. He sets it beside the insignia without pushing it toward you.
Accept the recommendation
You choose to begin as a Marine recruit, using his mistakes as warnings rather than excuses.
Keep the insignia without enlisting
You accept his family inheritance without making his profession your starting point.
Refuse both
You refuse to let his wish for you to do better become another expectation placed on you.
Your Answer
Your father no longer asks what you think of him. He asks what you want to do when Active begins.
event.family_marine_13_duty_not_obedienc: Open the report
You break the seal before anyone can summarize the contents for you.
Ask who paid for the report
You want to know whether the written truth cost a post, rank, or relationship.
Ask what you should do with it
You refuse to receive evidence without knowing whether it is also a responsibility.
Duty Is Not Obedience
Your father or a trusted Marine gives you a sealed report finally acknowledging that an order correct on paper endangered people. “Read it before you choose your future.”
Say it was worth the price
You accept that protection can sometimes cost the person who refuses.
Say the system should correct itself earlier
You reject heroic disobedience being the only way to get justice.
Say every refusal still needs judgment
You also refuse to turn every act of disobedience into automatic virtue.
The Price of Refusal
The file shows sanctions, testimony, and late corrections. Nobody comes out completely clean, but several people were protected because someone challenged the order.
State what you believe clearly
Your words oppose obedience and protection so sharply that your position is easy to caricature.
You know what you reject, but not yet how you would apply it day to day.
You clearly distinguish discipline, responsibility, and blind obedience.
Even the Marine facing you has to admit your position is neither a simple yes nor a simple no.
Keep your conclusion private
You refuse to turn your inheritance into a public declaration before Active even begins.
Ask whether the Marine truly accepts that position
You raise the contradiction before choosing the institution.
What You Take From the File
The report is now yours. You can keep it as evidence, warning, or a reason to join an institution you want to learn to challenge from within.
Join the Marine without promising blind obedience
You choose the Marine as a field of responsibility, not as surrender of your judgment.
Protect outside the uniform
You keep the ideal of protection while refusing to let one institution own it.
Keep the question open
You begin Active as a civilian with proof that the question can remain open later.
Serve or Protect Another Way
The report does not decide for you. It only proves the Marine can be challenged from within — and that protection also exists outside the uniform.
event.family_marine_13_our_name_is_not_t: Help return the symbols
You separate what belonged to the Marine from what still belongs to your family.
Take the report before they do
You make sure the family's version does not disappear with the official material.
Ask whether they want your name too
You make explicit the difference between leaving an institution and erasing an origin.
Our Name Is Not Theirs
After a public break, a Marine representative comes to collect documents and symbols loaned to the household. Your family still keeps a sealed report explaining why the break happened.
Say that is exactly the point
You accept losing the advantages that came with the expectation.
Say you have not rejected the idea of the Marine
You refuse to let the family break be interpreted as your final opinion.
Say your name remains yours
You refuse to let the institution turn separation into family shame.
What Is Actually Being Cut
The representative makes clear nobody can remove your family history. The break concerns access, recommendations, and professional expectations still attached to your name.
Remove your name
You choose to make the family break apply to your own Active start as well.
Keep your name on the list
You refuse to let breaking with how they treated your family prevent you from joining the Marine yourself.
Say you will decide without their list
You reject both automatic enrollment and automatic rejection.
The Last Form
The representative directly asks whether your name should also be removed from preparatory Active applications. That answer does not automatically belong to your family.
Begin Active outside the Marine
You turn the family break into a real professional separation when Active begins.
Join the Marine anyway
You reject how they treated your family, not the idea that you might wear the uniform differently.
Begin civilian without closing the door
You refuse to turn the break into a permanent professional identity.
Your Name, Your Decision
The official material leaves the household. The sealed report stays with you, proof the break happened without completely deciding what you do next.
event.family_marine_13_what_remains_of_h: Read the service pages first
You begin with the missions and choices he made in uniform.
Read the personal pages first
You begin with what he wrote when nobody asked him to represent the Marine.
Mix the pages
You refuse to artificially separate the man from the Marine before reading him.
What Remains of Him
After the plaque, the old sergeant brings you the last pages of your father's personal journal. “The wall keeps his name. This is what was left in his locker.”
Keep his service ideal
You refuse to let his contradictions erase the people he wanted to protect.
Keep the father first
You refuse to make rank the center of your memory.
Keep both without reconciling them
You accept that a memory can remain contradictory without becoming false.
The Memory You Choose
Some pages speak of duty, others of home. Several show your father himself did not always know where one ended and the other began.
Take the journal
You take the object containing his contradictions rather than one that summarizes them.
Copy only a few pages
You decide which parts of his story should actually travel with you.
Keep it all closed
You keep the journal without promising to reread it immediately.
One Object to Keep
Among his belongings, you choose the journal rather than an official symbol. It is the object that will stay with you after the ceremonies end.
Serve in his memory
You choose the Marine without pretending that choice completes or repairs your father's life.
Keep the father, not the profession
You keep his journal as inheritance and leave his uniform in his story.
Choose your own first path
You enter Active without asking his memory to choose your profession.
His Profession Is Not Your Answer
The old sergeant does not ask whether you want to become like him. He only asks whether the Marine is still part of your own answer.
event.family_marine_13_decide_for_yourse: Ask for advice, not a decision
You still accept adult experience without returning your choice to them.
Say you already know
You refuse to drag out a decision you have built for years.
Say you will not decide today
You treat delay as a legitimate decision too.
Decide for Yourself
After years of adults speaking about your name, body, or duty, the person beside you finally pushes all the forms away: “This answer has to come from you.”
Think about whom you want to protect
You turn inheritance into a concrete question rather than a symbol.
Think about what you refuse to surrender
You judge each option by what it demands from your autonomy.
Think about the price you accept
You refuse to choose only the most attractive image.
The Advice You Keep
You are given only one rule: choose a career whose consequences you will accept when nobody in your family is there to carry them with you.
Choose the Marine
You join the institution because you chose it after already questioning it.
Begin as a civilian
You want your first Active freedom to be owing no profession to your origin.
Defer commitment
You begin Active as a civilian and keep affiliations as future choices, not automatic inheritance.
The First Step Into Active
The field compass handed to you names no affiliation. You decide what your first Active status will say.
event.family_marine_13_your_name_on_roll: Read every line
You refuse to let family expectation move faster than your reading.
Make them explain the obligations
The officer answers in jargon and you need several points repeated.
You get the broad terms but some points remain vague.
The officer clearly explains duties, first posting, and the possibility of leaving later.
You get an ambiguous line corrected before anyone signs.
Close the register
You ask for the paper to stop being treated as an already settled conclusion.
Your Name on the Roll
The preparatory register is open to your name. An officer makes clear signing today gives no immediate rank: it prepares your entry as a recruit when Active begins.
Say you understand them
You agree to judge the Marine by its real obligations, not only its prestige.
Point out what worries you
You refuse to let discipline be a vague word answering every concern.
Say that is enough to refuse
You decide understanding the obligations can also be a reason not to sign.
The First Obligations
The officer reads what the register actually prepares: recruit training, discipline, initial posting, and a duty to answer orders once Active.
Look at your family one last time
You acknowledge everything that brought you here without asking them for the answer.
Ask one final confirmation
You make them repeat that you will begin at the first rank, with no rank privilege.
Look only at the line
You remove the choice from other people's gaze as much as possible.
Who Watches You Choose
Your father or the adults present stay behind you. The officer finally turns the register so the signature line faces only you.
Sign
You sign. Your Active start will begin in the Marine at recruit rank.
Put the pen down
You refuse to sign at the last moment without denying the history that brought you to it.
Ask them to leave the line blank
You do not sign today. If you return later, it will be a new decision.
The Signature
The pen is in your hand. This time, nobody can claim your name appeared on the roll without your choice.
event.family_marine_13_on_your_terms.cho: You first check what they actually kept from the previous agreement.
You refuse to let three years silently turn a boundary into a memory.
Say the offer still has to convince you
You remind them that an offer existing is not yet your consent.
event.family_marine_13_on_your_terms.tex: Three years after making them write your limits into their own file, the Marine returns with a Giant preparatory entry offer. This time, your conditions are printed beside theirs.
event.family_marine_13_on_your_terms_i01: You immediately point to where the institution is trying to reclaim room.
You refuse to negotiate over a sentence vague enough to authorize anything.
You acknowledge no agreement can predict every situation.
The program respects several limits: no demonstration without consent, training first, and adapted equipment. One new line, however, mentions “exceptional intervention by superior order.”
event.family_marine_13_on_your_terms_i02: You reject an exception that could swallow every previous boundary.
You accept emergency override only when it directly serves protecting people.
You accept that a Marine career sometimes requires duty beyond your consent in the moment.
The officer admits the clause could summon you without prior consent during a major crisis. He argues no special capability works without exceptions.
event.family_marine_13_on_your_terms_i03: Your wording is too broad and the officer refuses to write it as an operational rule.
He accepts the principle but not a clause binding enough to satisfy you.
You write an exception limited to immediate rescue with mandatory review afterward.
The clause distinguishes immediate rescue, military operation, and demonstration, precisely closing the abuses you feared.
You would rather lose the offer than leave an opening you believe cannot be controlled.
You choose this time to trust the people who will apply the text.
The file is nearly finished. The officer agrees to amend the clause only if you can state a limit precise enough to apply in the field.
event.family_marine_13_on_your_terms_i04: You enter the Marine with a file explicitly recognizing that your strength does not replace your judgment.
You prove that negotiating to the end never obligated you to accept. The decision remains yours.
You keep the future possibility but refuse to let even a good offer decide your first Active status.
The final offer is in front of you. You won the right to shape it, but nobody can make the final choice for you.
